script.text: On Tuesday, taps ran dry in parts of Kyiv after Russian strikes hit the power grid. Why do power plants keep becoming targets?

How much of Ukraine's electricity is already gone? Why is the grid a main target for both sides? And why has every energy truce so far fallen apart? One question from next week's Abu Dhabi talks stays open until the end.

Start with one number. Ukraine's electricity demand peaks at about twelve gigawatts, according to the International Energy Agency. Before the war, the country could cover that with room to spare. Then the invasion came. The agency says that over 2022 and 2023, about half of Ukraine's power generation capacity was occupied by Russian forces, destroyed or damaged. The occupation of the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant alone removed six gigawatts from the grid. About half of the large substations, the hubs that move electricity around the country, were damaged as well. Ukrainian authorities, cited by the Congressional Research Service, put the fall in available generation at fifty-one percent between early 2022 and April 2023. Many coal, gas and hydro plants have been hit since, and reports describe nuclear plants as now vital to the country's electricity. Imports from Europe, which Ukraine can use since it joined the European grid in March 2022, help to fill gaps. They cannot replace lost plants. For a family, that is the difference between a normal evening and one without light, heat or a working lift. If you want one of these explainers every Wednesday, subscribing is how you get it.

How fast can a grid be broken? Nine gigawatts, says the I.E.A. That is how much more generation Ukraine lost in just three months of strikes, between March and May 2024. It left Ukraine with about a third of its pre-war capacity. Ukraine's grid operator, Ukrenergo, gave a slightly lower estimate: more than eight gigawatts, about forty percent. By that summer, supply fell about two point three gigawatts short of peak demand, and Ukrenergo covered the gap with rolling blackouts. In 2025, Foreign Policy reported that Russian forces had destroyed or occupied about two thirds of Ukraine's pre-war generating capacity. Ukraine has since restored about three gigawatts. Every gigawatt rebuilt is a target again. And a repair crew works against the clock: a plant that took years to build can be disabled by one volley, and a replacement part can take months to arrive. That is why the winter months matter most. Heating demand rises, daylight falls, and every outage lasts longer in the cold.

So why does Russia keep hitting the grid? Moscow's position is that it strikes energy facilities that support Ukraine's army and military industry. Ukraine and many Western analysts point to the effect instead: darkness, cold and broken water pumps for millions of civilians, just as winter starts. What is clear is that the pattern has changed. The business outlet bne IntelliNews reports that Russia increasingly targets substations and transmission links, not only power plants. A substation can be repaired faster than a plant, but a hit on the right one switches off a whole region, even if the plants behind it are intact. Water pumps and heating systems in apartment blocks depend on that power. This week showed it. Quick question: how many times did Russia hit Ukrainian energy facilities in a single day? Take a guess. More than twenty times in twenty-four hours, says Ukrenergo. Emergency outages began in Kyiv and several regions, some lasting more than twelve hours. Kyiv's water utility said its main facilities lost power, and the mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said warming centers were opened in the worst-hit districts. And Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said three drones were aimed at a substation that is critical for the Khmelnytskyi nuclear plant.

Now the other side of the same war. Energy is a target in Russia too. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelensky, said Ukrainian forces struck fifteen Russian oil refineries between January and May this year. Ukraine's general staff claims that by early July, more than forty percent of Russia's refining capacity was out of action. That is a Ukrainian claim, and it has not been independently verified. Other estimates are lower. One Ukrainian outlet cites about thirty percent of actual capacity. What is documented is the reaction. Russia banned gasoline exports, and Bloomberg reported that Russian crude exports reached their highest level since the war began, because less oil was being refined at home. Reuters reported in May that drone strikes forced central Russian refineries to halt or cut output. A ban on gasoline exports, announced by Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, began on April first. On Friday, Moscow accused Kyiv of resuming refinery strikes despite a request from Donald Trump to stop. Ukraine's argument is that refineries feed the army. Russia's argument is that Kyiv is the one breaking the truce. For drivers in Russia, that means shortages. For the rest of us, it means a war that now reaches fuel markets.

If both sides keep losing energy, why not stop? They tried. On March eighteenth, 2025, after a phone call between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, the Kremlin announced a thirty-day halt on strikes against energy targets. Moscow said it began that day. Kyiv said it began a week later. Within days, each side accused the other of breaking it. On March twenty-eighth, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia reserved the right to stop complying if Kyiv did. On April eighteenth, the Kremlin said the pause had expired. Then, on October eleventh this year, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire. A source close to Zelensky called the announcement a surprise. Russia has not confirmed an agreement. Days later, Zelensky said Russia hit power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions in one night, and Russia's Defense Ministry said it downed two hundred and thirty-five Ukrainian drones, while the governor of Nizhny Novgorod reported an industrial site hit. Each side says the other started it. And the Financial Times reported in September that Putin does not want a deal to halt energy strikes before winter. The Kremlin even published a list of facilities covered by that first pause, and it included oil refineries and nuclear power plants. That is the reporter's account, and the Kremlin has not commented on it in the sources we found.

What happens next could start on November tenth. U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff says Russia, Ukraine and the United States will meet in Abu Dhabi on November tenth and eleventh. The Kremlin has confirmed it will take part. Witkoff says the agenda covers security arrangements, easing the fighting and humanitarian steps, and one report adds a possible energy and maritime ceasefire. Here are the scenarios that sources describe. First, a limited energy deal: lights stay on in Ukrainian cities through the coldest months, and refineries stop burning in Russia. Second, a wider package. Witkoff's agenda includes de-escalation, and the Moscow Times notes that Putin's only apparent concession so far is agreeing to resume talks. Third, no deal. The New York Times reported on October sixteenth that Russia is planning winter strikes to cut electricity, heat and water in Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa. That is a reported plan, not a confirmed event. So what is the open question? Who checks that the strikes have really stopped? In 2025, both sides said they kept the deal and the other side broke it. Will Russia and Ukraine agree to stop energy strikes before January? Tell us in the comments: yes or no.
Next, we follow the money behind Russia's war: how sanctions on oil actually work, what the price cap does, and who pays for the shadow fleet. Watch that one next.

upload.title: Why Russia Keeps Hitting Ukraine's Power Grid
upload.description:
Why do power plants keep becoming targets in the war in Ukraine? This explainer shows how much of Ukraine's electricity generation has been lost, why Russia strikes substations and power plants, how Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries fit in, why the 2025 energy-strike pause and the October 2026 energy ceasefire announcement did not hold, and what sources say could come out of the Abu Dhabi talks on November 10 and 11. Claims are attributed to their sources; disputed or unverified claims are labelled.
